name: Ensoniq Mirage
originalPurpose: A sampling keyboard at a price a working musician could actually reach, at a moment when sampling otherwise meant a Fairlight and the cost of a house.
whatActuallyHappened: It sold nearly eight thousand units in its first year, more than every other sampler on the market combined, and put recording-and-replaying sound into ordinary bedrooms. Its eight-bit sampling was noisy and its memory was tiny, neither of which turned out to matter. Derrick May built 'Strings of Life' on one, out of a piano part his friend Michael James had played at his house, sped up and cut into loops.
priceStory: 1,695 US dollars at launch, against five figures for the samplers it was competing with. The gap between those two numbers is the reason a Detroit teenager could own one.
hook: The sampler that cost as much as a used car rather than as much as a house.

blurb.age7: A keyboard that could record any sound and let you play it back on the keys, cheap enough that ordinary people could buy one.
blurb.age13: Sampling means recording a sound and then playing it back at different pitches from a keyboard. Until 1984 the machines that did it cost more than a house, so only famous studios had them. The Mirage cost about as much as a used car. It was noisy and could only hold a couple of seconds, and it still sold more in its first year than every other sampler put together, because being able to afford it mattered more than being good.
blurb.adult: The Mirage is where sampling stops being an elite studio technique and becomes a common compositional method. Its technical limits, eight-bit resolution and very short memory, pushed users toward short loops and hard edits, which is a constraint the records of the following decade are audibly shaped by rather than in spite of.
